name: Febrile Infection-Related Epilepsy Syndrome
aliases: Acute Encephalopathy with Refractory, Recurrent Status Epilepticus (AERRS)

criteria.description: History of febrile infection 2 weeks to 24 hours prior to onset of refractory status epilepticus
New onset of refractory status epilepticus without clear structural, toxic, or metabolic cause
Exclusion of other causes such as CNS infection, autoimmune encephalitis, or metabolic disorders
Typical onset in previously healthy children or young adults
EEG showing multifocal seizures or status epilepticus

diagnosticCriteria.minimumForDiagnosis: Presence of refractory status epilepticus following a febrile illness with exclusion of other causes
diagnosticCriteria.notes: Diagnosis is clinical and by exclusion; no definitive biomarker currently available

laboratory: Mild to moderate elevation of inflammatory markers (e.g., CRP, ESR)
Normal or mildly elevated CSF protein with no pleocytosis
imaging: MRI brain may show T2/FLAIR hyperintensities in limbic structures or diffuse cortical abnormalities
Possible cerebral edema in acute phase
Later brain atrophy in chronic phase
genetic: No consistent genetic mutations identified; some cases show variants in epilepsy-related genes but no definitive association
other: EEG shows multifocal seizures or generalized status epilepticus

distinguishingFeatures: Identification of infectious agent in CSF or blood
Fever and seizures directly related to active infection
Early onset seizures without preceding febrile illness
Genetic testing positive for pathogenic variants
Chronic developmental delay prior to seizure onset

redFlags: Prolonged refractory status epilepticus unresponsive to standard treatment
Rapid neurological deterioration following febrile illness
Development of super-refractory status epilepticus requiring anesthetic agents
references: Nabbout R, et al. Febrile infection-related epilepsy syndrome (FIRES): Pathogenesis, treatment, and outcome. Epilepsia. 2017.
van Baalen A, et al. Febrile infection-related epilepsy syndrome (FIRES): Pathophysiology and treatment. Epilepsia. 2018.
Wong-Kisiel LC, et al. Febrile infection-related epilepsy syndrome: A review. J Child Neurol. 2019.
